title: Essential ingredients
description: Explore the components that let an AI agent perceive its environment, decide what to do, and learn from the outcome.

root.title: Essential ingredients
root.summary: How an agent senses, thinks, acts, and adapts.

data.text: An AI agent operates in a loop: it receives information, interprets the situation, chooses an action, changes its environment, and observes the result.

data.label: The loop
data.text: Perceive → interpret → decide → act → observe

children.title: Environment
children.summary: The world the agent perceives and interacts with.

data.text: An environment may be physical, digital, or a combination. It contains the conditions, systems, and other actors that can affect the agent's goal.

items: Physical: roads, vehicles, people, signs, and weather
Digital: stores, catalogs, prices, reviews, and user preferences
Combined: digital information alongside location, season, or local conditions

children.title: Dynamic conditions
children.summary: The world can change while the agent is working.

data.text: Agents often work in environments where relevant facts change over time. A plan based on an earlier observation can become stale before it is carried out.

items: Identify which conditions can change.
Decide how often the agent needs fresh observations.
Re-check important facts before consequential actions.

data.label: Example
data.text: A shopping assistant should check current stock and price before it recommends a product as available.

children.title: Define the boundary
children.summary: Specify which parts of the world are relevant to this task.

data.text: A clear boundary identifies the systems, people, time horizon, and conditions that matter. It also helps exclude unrelated or sensitive information.

children.title: Scope checklist
children.summary: Make the operating context explicit before choosing sensors or tools.

items: What entities and conditions can affect the goal?
Which sources are authoritative and current?
What information is unnecessary or sensitive?
Which changes require the agent to reassess its plan?

children.title: Test a missing-context case
children.summary: Define what the agent does when a required fact is unavailable.

data.text: A robust environment model identifies missing or stale context as a condition to handle. The agent can retrieve updated information, ask the user, or stop before taking an unsafe action.

children.title: Physical and digital examples
children.summary: Different tasks place the agent in different kinds of worlds.

data.text: Self-driving car
Road layout, traffic, pedestrians, weather, and traffic signs all form part of the car's environment.
Shopping assistant
Product catalogs, user preferences, prices, reviews, promotions, weather, and season can all influence a recommendation.

children.title: Sensors
children.summary: The channels through which the agent gathers input.

data.text: Sensors are the means by which an agent receives information from its environment. They turn signals into observations the agent can process.

items: Web scrapers and search tools
APIs and database connections
Cameras, microphones, LiDAR, and GPS
IoT devices and other live data integrations

children.title: Physical sensors
children.summary: Devices that measure the physical world.

data.text: Physical agents combine sensors because each captures different evidence and has different limitations.

items: Cameras capture visual scenes and signs.
LiDAR estimates distance and surrounding geometry.
GPS provides location signals.
Microphones capture audio; vehicle systems provide additional state readings.

data.label: Design check
data.text: Consider sensor coverage, delay, calibration, obstruction, and what the agent should do when a signal is unreliable.

children.title: Digital inputs
children.summary: Software tools that retrieve information from online systems.

data.text: A shopping agent may use web scrapers for product information, APIs for browsing history, comparison modules for prices, and integrations for live weather.

children.title: Input quality and freshness
children.summary: Collected data can be incomplete, delayed, or contradictory.

data.text: The model can only reason from the evidence it receives. Sources, timestamps, permissions, and validation all affect how much an observation should be trusted.

items: Track where an observation came from.
Check whether it is recent enough for the task.
Detect missing or conflicting values.
Ask for clarification or pause if critical inputs are uncertain.

children.title: Model
children.summary: The component that interprets observations and forms an understanding.

data.text: Collecting data is only the first step. A model processes perceptions, recognizes context, and helps the agent understand what may be happening.

items: Machine-learning algorithms for focused tasks
Neural networks for complex patterns
Large language models for language-based reasoning
Multimodal models that combine text, images, audio, or video

children.title: Model capability
children.summary: Choose a model that fits the information and task.

data.text: Models range in sophistication. A focused classifier may be enough for a narrow decision, while a multimodal language model can interpret several kinds of information together.

data.label: Remember
data.text: A model's interpretation is evidence for a decision, not proof that an action is safe, authorized, or correct.

children.title: Multimodal context
children.summary: Use multiple input forms to build a richer understanding.

data.text: Text, images, audio, and video can be considered together. This can improve context awareness in complex environments, but each modality also introduces uncertainty.

children.title: Context and uncertainty
children.summary: Treat model output as an interpretation that may need checking.

data.text: Models may lack current facts, misunderstand ambiguous inputs, or produce plausible but unsupported answers. Important claims should be grounded in trusted evidence.

items: Retrieve current information when freshness matters.
Keep source evidence available for review.
Escalate uncertain, high-impact cases.

children.title: Decision logic
children.summary: Rules and objectives that guide the agent's choice of action.

data.text: Decision logic evaluates options and turns model output into a choice. It can be a structured algorithm, explicit rules, or a thin external layer around an LLM.

data.label: Why add a layer?
data.text: External checks can enforce safety, legal, and business constraints that a model's own instructions should not override.

children.title: Rules and thresholds
children.summary: Translate probabilistic model output into consistent actions.

data.text: A spam filter can classify a message as spam only when the model's estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold. A trading rule can reject investments outside specified return or volatility limits.

items: Make the condition explicit.
Measure the cost of false positives and false negatives.
Provide review for uncertain cases.

children.title: Safety and authorization
children.summary: Verify constraints independently before consequential actions.

data.text: An external logic layer can verify transaction limits, authentication, permissions, or legal requirements before an action is allowed.

children.title: Human confirmation
children.summary: Pause for a person when the action is unclear or high impact.

data.text: The agent can request confirmation when it cannot confidently distinguish among actions or when consequences require human authority.

items: Explain the proposed action.
Show the relevant evidence and consequences.
Wait for explicit approval before execution.

children.title: Actions & tools
children.summary: The mechanisms the agent uses to affect its environment.

data.text: Agents interact with their environment through actuators or tools. Physical agents may move a robotic arm or control steering and braking; digital agents may use functions, APIs, browsers, and integrations.

items: Read-only tools retrieve information.
Write tools change external state.
Some actions have side effects that are difficult to undo.

children.title: Tool use
children.summary: Connect the selected action to a well-defined tool.

data.text: The model may propose an action, but the agent needs a tool with an explicit interface to carry it out and return an observable result.

data.label: Email example
data.text: An email agent can classify a message, move it to spam, flag an attachment, or ask the user when the correct action is unclear.

children.title: Permissions and side effects
children.summary: Limit what each tool can access and change.

data.text: Use the least access needed, validate tool inputs, and distinguish a requested operation from one that has actually succeeded.

children.title: Verify the result
children.summary: Observe the external state after an action.

data.text: Tool calls can fail, partially complete, time out, or be repeated. Check the resulting state before telling the user an operation is complete.

items: Handle retries carefully.
Confirm important state changes.
Report partial completion honestly.

children.title: Feedback loop
children.summary: How the agent observes outcomes and improves future behavior.

data.text: Actions create new conditions. Sensors receive fresh information about the updated environment, which can reveal whether the agent achieved its intended goal.

data.label: Core idea
data.text: The agent does not stop at acting: it observes the outcome and decides whether another step is needed.

children.title: Observe the updated state
children.summary: Collect new input after acting.

data.text: The updated environment provides new observations. These are processed and compared with the intended result, closing the basic agent loop.

items: Perform the action.
Receive updated sensor input.
Check the result against the goal.
Choose another action or stop.

children.title: Learning and adaptation
children.summary: Use relevant outcomes to improve later choices.

data.text: Repeated observations can help refine behavior over time. Adaptation may be as simple as remembering a preference, or as involved as evaluating and updating a model.

children.title: Everyday examples
children.summary: Feedback makes future behavior more relevant to the user.

data.text: A thermostat can learn from manual temperature changes. A recommendation system can use what a person watches, skips, pauses, or rates to tailor future suggestions.

items: Decide what information is retained.
Respect privacy and user preferences.
Measure whether adaptation improves outcomes.
